summary: The first part of Privacy Enhanced Mail. It describes message encipherment and authentication procedures for private electronic mail. It is historic and was replaced by RFC 1421.

eli5.summary: This is a way to put your email in a locked box and sign it, so only the right person can read it and they know it came from you.

subtitle: How to encrypt and authenticate Internet electronic mail so recipients know the message is real and unopened.

tldr.problem: Electronic mail passes through many computers on the Internet where it can be read or modified. Users need a way to prove they wrote a message and to keep it secret from anyone except the intended recipient.
tldr.mechanism: PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail) adds encryption and digital signatures to email at the application layer, independent of the mail transport system. A sender encrypts the message with a random key (DEK) and encrypts that key for each recipient with their key (IK). Special headers carry the encrypted keys. The recipient uses their key to decrypt the DEK, then uses it to decrypt the message.
tldr.outcome: Users could send secure email across the Internet without modifying email servers or relying on encryption at lower layers. However, PEM saw limited adoption due to key management complexity. RFC 1421 is the successor document.

facts.label: Encoding
facts.value: Base64 or equivalent, restricted to 7-bit ASCII

today: RFC 1113 is part of the PEM (Privacy Enhanced Mail) series and is Historic. RFC 1421 superseded it with improved terminology and procedures. Modern secure email uses S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), which combines public-key cryptography with the Internet's certificate infrastructure (X.509), making encryption easier to adopt than PEM required.

sections.title: The Challenge of Secure Email
sections.content:
RFC 1113 is the first part of Privacy Enhanced Mail, a protocol for adding encryption and authentication to Internet electronic mail. It defines message encipherment and authentication procedures while working within the constraints of the existing SMTP email system.

The core challenge is that email passes through many intermediate systems (Message Transfer Agents, or MTAs) that may convert character sets, change line endings, or modify the message in other ways. Any encryption or encoding must survive this process unchanged. Additionally, the solution must work without modifying mail servers themselves; the security processing must happen in user agents (mail client applications) or in separate tools.

PEM supports both symmetric cryptography (where sender and recipient share a secret key) and asymmetric cryptography (where recipients have public keys and senders have private keys). Asymmetric approaches allow any two parties to communicate securely without prior key exchange, making them more practical for Internet email.
sections.eli5: Email goes through many computers before it reaches you. Some might try to read it. You need a way to lock it so only your friend can open it, even though it passes through untrusted mail systems.

sections.title: Two-Level Key Hierarchy
sections.content:
PEM uses two types of encryption keys. A Data Encrypting Key (DEK) is a random key generated fresh for each message. It encrypts the message text and, if the algorithm requires it, a message integrity check (MIC). Using a new DEK for each message limits the damage if one key is stolen.

An Interchange Key (IK) is a long-term key used to encrypt the DEK for transmission. In symmetric mode, the IK is a secret key shared between the sender and each recipient, established out-of-band (via secure phone call, in person, or other private means). In asymmetric mode with public keys, the IK is the recipient's public key (for encrypting the DEK) and the sender's private key (for signing the MIC).

For each recipient of a message, the sender includes the DEK encrypted under that recipient's key. The recipient retrieves their encrypted DEK from the message headers, decrypts it using their key, then uses the DEK to decrypt the message. This approach allows one message to be addressed to multiple recipients without encrypting the message text multiple times.
sections.eli5: You create a random key for this message only. You lock that key in a separate small box for each friend, using their personal key. They unlock their small box to get the message key, then use it to read your letter.

sections.title: Four-Step Message Transformation
sections.content:
An outbound privacy-enhanced message undergoes four transformations. Step 1: Local Form. The sender creates the message in their system's native character set and line-ending convention (for example, UNIX uses LF, while Windows uses CR-LF).

Step 2: Canonical Form. The entire message is converted to a universal representation: 7-bit ASCII with CR-LF line endings, matching the inter-SMTP standard from RFC 821 and 822. This ensures the message is portable and that any signature or MIC computed on it will match at the recipient's end, regardless of local conventions.

Step 3: Authentication and Encryption. The canonical message is used to compute a Message Integrity Check (MIC, also called a digest or hash), which proves no one modified the message. The message (or portions of it) is then encrypted with the DEK using DES in CBC mode. The sender may exclude portions of the message from encryption while still authenticating the entire message.

Step 4: Printable Encoding. The encrypted text is encoded into a form that will survive email transport: base64 (or another compatible encoding) that uses only 7-bit ASCII characters and respects mail system line-length limits (1000 characters per line). The original regions excluded from encryption remain as plaintext but encoded in the same format.

When the recipient receives the message, they reverse these steps: decode from printable form, decrypt encrypted regions, verify the MIC, and convert from canonical form to their local representation.
sections.eli5: 1. You write it on your computer. 2. Convert it to a universal format (like translating to a common language). 3. Sign it and lock it with your random key. 4. Encode it so it can travel through email. The recipient reverses all four steps.

sections.title: Headers and Message Format
sections.content:
PEM-enhanced messages include new mail headers (field names beginning with "X-") that carry cryptographic control information. The X-Proc-Type field identifies the message as privacy-enhanced and indicates its version. The X-DEK-Info field specifies which encryption algorithm was used (e.g., "DES-CBC") and provides the initialization vector (IV).

The X-Sender-ID field identifies the sender and the sender's key, allowing the recipient to locate the appropriate sender's public certificate. For each recipient, an X-Recipient-ID field names that recipient's key, followed by an X-Key-Info field containing the message's DEK encrypted under that recipient's interchange key.

An X-Certificate field can carry the sender's public key certificate, and X-Issuer-Certificate fields can carry intermediate certificates needed to verify the sender's certificate. An X-MIC-Info field (in asymmetric mode) carries the message's integrity check encrypted under the sender's private key, providing non-repudiation: the sender cannot later claim they did not write the message.

The encapsulated headers are followed by a blank line, then the encoded message text. This structure allows the message to be processed by privacy-enhanced mail readers while remaining visible to older mail systems as an ordinary message with unusual headers and encoded text.
sections.eli5: The message has special headers (X-Proc-Type, X-DEK-Info, X-Recipient-ID, X-Key-Info) that tell the recipient what encryption was used and how to find the message key locked in their box.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content:
RFC 1113 is part of a four-RFC series: Part I defines message procedures (this document), Part II (RFC 1114) defines key management using public-key certificates, Part III (RFC 1115) specifies algorithms and codes, and Part IV (RFC 1116) provides syntax examples. Together they form a complete privacy enhancement system for Internet mail.

Although technically sound, PEM faced practical adoption barriers. The key management infrastructure required was complex and centralized. Users preferred simpler email encryption systems like PGP (Pretty Good Privacy), which operated independently of any central authority. RFC 1421 replaced PEM with similar procedures but simplified terminology and structure. Modern systems typically use S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions), which builds on similar principles but with better integration into email systems and the Web's public key infrastructure.
sections.eli5: This was one of the first standards for secure email. It was replaced by RFC 1421. Today people use systems like S/MIME that work similarly but are easier to use.
